Verify rewrite DATA ONLY. Do not write improved examples or solve the user's task.
Read every input and target in full. Return one review per exact id and row_sha256.
input_verdict checks plausible natural drafts or dictation, recoverable intent, contradictions,
fake noise, padding and leaked authoring instructions. output_verdict checks natural appropriate
language and formatting. pair_verdict checks ALL facts, uncertainty, conditions, negation,
quantities, names, quotations, literals, requests versus assertions, and the supplied mode.
/transcribe permits punctuation, true disfluency removal and explicit corrections, not lexical
paraphrasing. Preserve meaningful words like German 'um' and 'er', colloquial Portuguese and
unfinished thoughts. /slack is casual minimal cleanup; a long input may be a pasted thread.
/prompt reorganizes a self-contained request and never answers it. It must not drop supplied
material, hedges or constraints. /polish improves prose without omissions or changed certainty.
Identity inputs must remain byte-identical. Apply only supplied dictionary/profile context.
Check long texts paragraph by paragraph. Fail concrete defects. Uncertain means not confidently
justifiable. Pass requires no material defect. Overall verdict is fail if any dimension fails,
uncertain if any dimension is uncertain and none fails, otherwise pass. Give a concrete critique
for EVERY pair, citing the changed detail for defects. These are model judgments, not human labels.

Do not perform the task.", "input": "Develop a discussion-question guide for a fictional independent radio episode about collecting vinyl. The episode is called “Side A, Side B,” and it brings together four collectors for a recorded conversation at Needle & Pine, a small record shop in the fictional town of Bellwether. The shop has been open for eleven years, sells used and new records, and holds listening nights in a narrow back room with a green sofa and a turntable connected to two mismatched speakers. The guide is for a host who wants the guests to tell specific stories, compare different habits, and disagree comfortably where their experiences differ. Write useful, open-ended questions, not answers, summaries, or a script.

The guests have distinct collecting histories. Mara Chen, 34, began buying records at campus record fairs and now keeps around 260 LPs in a third-floor apartment. She listens mostly to soul and contemporary jazz, labels sleeves with the month she bought them, and avoids grading records above her budget. Leon Price, 61, started collecting in the late 1970s, has roughly 1,400 records in alphabetized shelves, and says he is more interested in local labels and liner notes than in owning rare pressings. His first record was a used copy of Stevie Wonder’s Songs in the Key of Life, which he bought with money from a summer job. Ask questions that make room for their different ages and collecting priorities without treating either person as representative of a whole generation.

The other two guests bring different perspectives. Inez Alvarez, 47, inherited about 90 records from her aunt, including salsa, boleros, and several albums with handwritten notes inside the sleeves. She has since added records from flea markets and shops, but she is still deciding which inherited items feel like hers to keep and which she might pass to cousins. Theo Grant, 28, buys a mix of punk, electronic music, and soundtracks, and shares a rented house with two friends. He has about 180 records, stores some in milk crates, and uses a spreadsheet to track purchase price, condition, and where he found each one. Include questions that let Inez talk about memory and family without assuming every inherited record has sentimental value, and let Theo explain his practical system without making it sound like a joke.

The conversation should touch on the ordinary decisions and compromises that shape a collection. Guests have mentioned limited shelf space, the cost of new reissues, used-record grading, warped discs, surface noise, dust, inner sleeves, and the challenge of deciding when a record is worth repairing. Mara recently passed on a clean-looking copy of an album because the price tag was far beyond her limit; Leon once bought a scuffed local pressing after hearing that it included an alternate track; Inez found one of her aunt’s records with a note on the back of the sleeve; Theo has had to reorganize his spreadsheet after moving twice. Use questions to draw out concrete examples and differing standards. Avoid implying that buying expensive or rare records is the best kind of collecting.

Include the social side of the hobby as well. Needle & Pine’s listening nights usually draw between eight and fifteen people, and attendees take turns choosing one side of an album to play. Some guests at those nights bring records to trade, while others arrive mainly to listen. The shop’s owner, Della Brooks, has noticed that first-time visitors sometimes feel unsure whether they are allowed to touch the records or ask for help. A neighborhood library recently asked Needle & Pine to suggest records for a small “music and memory” display, but no selections have been made yet. Ask about sharing recommendations, trading, listening together, and helping newcomers feel welcome, without turning the discussion into a promotion for the shop or library.

Ask about how people find records and judge their condition. The guests use different routes: record shops, fairs, online listings, estate sales, and recommendations from friends. They may have different ways of checking a sleeve, looking for scratches, reading a pressing label, or deciding whether to buy an album without hearing it first. Include questions about a lucky find as well as a purchase that did not meet expectations. Keep the questions neutral about digital music; the episode is focused on vinyl collecting, but the guests should not be pushed to claim that records sound better or matter more than other formats. Do not assume all four guests collect for the same reason or listen to every record they own.

Organize the guide into a brief opening section, a numbered main section, and a short closing section. The numbered section should contain about twelve to sixteen questions, arranged in a natural progression from first memories and discovery to storage, spending, listening, and what might change in the future. Vary the questions so they do not all begin with the same phrase. Include several follow-up prompts that invite a particular moment, object, sound, or decision, but keep the guide usable in a live conversation. Questions should be concise enough to read aloud and open enough that guests can answer in their own way. Do not require every guest to answer every question; suggest where a question could be directed to one or two guests based on their stated experience.

Keep the tone curious, relaxed, and respectful. Ordinary disagreement about condition, value, or the best way to organize records is welcome, but avoid framing collecting as a competition or diagnosing anyone’s spending. Do not add biographical details, records, shop events, or outcomes beyond the information provided here. Do not write the episode itself, invent guest quotations, supply conclusions, or include answers beneath the questions. material from my notebook and the short interview:

The episode follows Lena Ortiz, who has been collecting records for about six years and lives in Bellwether, a fictional town with two record shops and a weekend flea market. She works mornings at a bakery and says she does not have room for a large collection. At the start of the episode she counts 143 records in her apartment, though she says a few are duplicates that she intends to trade. Her interest began when her aunt gave her a used copy of Joni Mitchell's Blue. The sleeve was worn, and Lena says, “I liked that it had belonged to somebody before me.” She still owns the copy, but does not claim it is especially rare.

Most Saturdays, Lena visits North Loop Records, a shop run by Dev Shah. The episode shows her checking the used bins before looking at new arrivals. Dev says the shop prices records by condition and demand, and that a familiar album is not automatically valuable. Lena picks up a copy of Talking Heads' Remain in Light, checks the jacket seams, then puts it back after noticing a split along the top edge. She tells the camera, “I want to play the records, not keep them sealed like a display.” Dev mentions that customers sometimes ask for a discount after spotting wear, but that he writes the condition on the tag so they can decide before buying. Lena leaves without making a purchase that morning.

A second visit is to the Bellwether flea market, where Lena meets her friend Omar Bell near a stall of used books and records. Omar collects jazz albums and has been trying to find a particular pressing of a Thelonious Monk record. He says he has checked the market several times, but he is not certain the pressing turns up there often. At the stall, Lena finds a worn copy of Fleetwood Mac's Rumours for four dollars. The seller, June Park, says she has not tested it on a turntable and does not know whether it plays cleanly. Lena looks at the label and sleeve, then asks if she can listen to it before paying. June says there is no player at the market, so Lena decides to leave it. Omar says, “Four dollars is cheap, but cheap isn't the same as a good copy.” They continue looking at other stalls and do not find the Monk pressing.

In the kitchen at home, Lena explains how she decides what to buy. She keeps a handwritten list in a small notebook, but says it is a guide rather than a rule. The episode shows three entries she has crossed off after finding copies elsewhere: a used copy of Nina Simone's Pastel Blues, a reissue of an album by the Cure, and a compilation whose title is partly obscured in the shot. She says she does not want the summary to imply she bought any of those records during the episode; they're on the list as past searches. She also describes trading duplicates with other collectors rather than selling them for cash. One duplicate is a second copy of a record she already owns, but the notebook does not identify the title.

There is a numbered section in my notes from the interview, which i think should be included in some form:
1. Lena tries to keep purchases to one or two records a month, but says this changes if she finds something she has been searching for.
2. She looks for clean playback, intact sleeves, and prices she can afford; she does not rank rarity above those things.
3. She sometimes listens to a record in full before deciding whether it belongs in her collection.

Later, Dev says new collectors can feel pressure to buy quickly when a record is described as scarce. He says, “If you're unsure, it's fine to go home and think about it.” The episode does not say that Lena follows this advice every time, only that she agrees with the general point. Near the end, she cleans a record at home with a carbon-fiber brush before putting it on her turntable. The label is not shown clearly enough to identify the album. She listens while writing a note about its condition in her notebook. In the final conversation, Lena says collecting gives her “a reason to pay attention,” and explains that she likes learning how different copies sound, not just filling shelves. Please summarize what happens, include the key buying decisions and the different views of Lena, Dev, and Omar, and keep the uncertainty about the flea-market record and the unidentified album intact.
